title: Nepal PM Balen Shah says won't remove sunglasses in Parliament. Here's why - India Today
description: Nepal PM Balen Shah says won't remove sunglasses in Parliament. Here's why  India Today
publisher.title: India Today
full_article:
Summoned by the Speaker, Nepal Prime Minister Balendra 'Balen' Shah will appear in Parliament on Wednesday (August 26). However, lawmakers who got the PM to attend the proceedings, won't be able to see eye to eye with him. The reason: Balen Shah will keep his dark sunglasses on even in Parliament.

Use of dark glasses was prohibited in Parliament by Speaker Dol Prasad Aryal but Balen Shah has found a way around.

Nepali media outlets reported on Tuesday that an ophthalmologist had suggested that Balen Shah wear dark sunglasses to protect his eye and use eyedrops.

Shah had gone for a check-up at the Birendra Military Hospital in Chhauni and was reviewed by Associate Professor Lieutenant Colonel Dr Sachit Dhakal, according to The Kathmandu Post.

The doctor diagnosed him with light sensitivity and dry eyes, prescribing regular eye drops and protective dark glasses, reported Nepal News.

The news outlets reported that the PMO forwarded Balen Shah's medical report and doctors' recommendations to the Federal Parliament Secretariat.

Shah is scheduled to take direct questions from lawmakers and the report of the medical examination comes just a day ahead of that.

The dark glasses have been part of the persona of Balen Shah, a rapper-turned-politician, who is heading a majority government after years in Nepal. The Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP), which fielded Shah, has a near two-thirds majority.

Shah was propelled to the PM's post after Gen Z protesters overthrew the KP Sharma Oli government in September 2025. While the youngsters see the dark glasses among Balen Shah's defiance, the Nepal PM's critics see it as a mark of his arrogance.

Shah has come in for criticism for his personality-based politics and undermining of democratic institutions and diplomatic norms. Even as he completed the first 150 days as PM, Shah seems to have lost much of his political shine.

Experts have slammed Shah for his confrontational attitude and concentrating power in his hands.

Balen Shah is "alienating constituencies that any government eventually needs: the media, the intelligentsia, the opposition parties and key foreign partners", wrote Biswas Baral, the former Editor of The Kathmandu Post, for The Diplomat in June.

In a recent column in The Kathmandu Times, analyst Samar SJB Rana asked whether Nepal, after overthrowing one political order, risks replacing it with something equally dependent on one personality. "Nepal wants no Caesar," he wrote.

The reference was to Julius Caesar, a symbol of absolute power and autocracy.

His refusal to take off the shades, despite providing a medical certificate, will be seen as another instance of his defiance.

Speaker Dol Prasad Aryal had on August 6 told political parties to inform their lawmakers that dark sunglasses wouldn't be permitted during Parliament proceedings except for medical reasons, reported The Kathmandu Post.

Balen Shah, forced by Nepal's lawmakers, will be attending House proceedings but he will keep wearing his trademark sunglasses.

title: Nepal defeats Malaysia by 9 wickets in practice match - Ratopati
description: Nepal defeats Malaysia by 9 wickets in practice match  Ratopati
publisher.title: Ratopati
full_article:
Kathmandu. Nepal has won the practice match against Malaysia by 9 wickets. In the match affected by rain, Nepal was given a target of 228 runs in 48 overs according to the Duckworth-Lewis (DLS) method.

On Tuesday, Nepal achieved the target in 28 overs by losing one wicket. Asif Sheikh batted excellently for Nepal, scoring 161 runs in 85 balls. He hit 12 fours and 12 sixes in his innings.

Similarly, Arjun Kumal scored 61 runs in 82 balls. He hit 7 fours. Dev Khanal remained unbeaten on one run.

Earlier, Malaysia, after winning the toss and batting first, lost all wickets in 48.2 overs, scoring 232 runs in the stipulated 50 overs.

Among Nepal's bowlers, SA Mubarak spent 18 runs in 3 overs but could not take a wicket. Malaysia's Arif Ullah spent 13 runs in 4 overs, V Yu Suresh spent 19 runs in 4 overs, P Madhukar spent 24 runs in 3 overs, Mohammad Amir spent 32 runs in 2 overs, and Amir Khan Malik spent 23 runs in 3 overs.

Similarly, A Wahid spent 37 runs in 4 overs, Bishwaruven Kumar spent 21 runs in 2 overs, and Saifullah Malik spent 23 runs in 2 overs. Aslam Khan Malik spent 19 runs in 1 over and took one wicket.

Although Malaysia scored 232 runs, Nepal was given a revised target of 228 runs in 48 overs. Before going to Malaysia, Nepal played two practice matches against Karnataka in India.

Nepal had won both matches. Nepal has gone to Malaysia to play the ACC Premier Cup starting August 30. Nepal played the practice match as preparation for it.

title: Nepal crush Malaysia in ACC Premier Cup warm-up - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepal crush Malaysia in ACC Premier Cup warm-up  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Nepal beat Malaysia by nine wickets in a rain-affected practice match ahead of the ACC Men’s Premier Cup, powered by a century from opener Aasif Sheikh and a half-century from Arjun Kumal.



Malaysia, who won the toss and elected to bat, were bowled out for 232 in 48.2 overs.

Rain interrupted Nepal’s chase, reducing their target to 228 from 48 overs under the Duckworth-Lewis-Stern method. Nepal reached the revised target in just 28 overs, losing only one wicket.

Sheikh smashed 161 from 85 balls, hitting 12 sixes and 12 fours in a blistering innings. He and Kumal put on 220 for the first wicket, giving Nepal a dominant start.

Kumal remained unbeaten on 61 from 82 balls, hitting seven fours.

For Malaysia, Muhammad Ramli top-scored with 61, while Saif Ullah Malik made 45 and Syed Aziz scored 40.

Nepal captain Sandeep Lamichhane was the pick of the bowlers, taking four wickets for 36 runs from 10 overs. Karan KC took two wickets, while Lalit Rajbanshi and Dipendra Singh Airee claimed one each.

The ACC Men’s Premier Cup 2026 will be held in Malaysia from August 30 to September 12. Nepal and Malaysia are in the same group at the ACC Premier Cup, alongside Bahrain, Hong Kong and Saudi Arabia.

Nepal will play Bahrain in its opening match on Monday.

title: A TikTok video from the India-Nepal border area showed a pale fish with reduced eyes that had come out of a borewell, and the researchers who went looking hand-pumped more than 15 of them in about a week to get three specimens, enough to describe wh - Space Daily
description: A TikTok video from the India-Nepal border area showed a pale fish with reduced eyes that had come out of a borewell, and the researchers who went looking hand-pumped more than 15 of them in about a week to get three specimens, enough to describe wh  Space Daily
publisher.title: Space Daily
full_article:
A fish with no scientific name came out of a hand pump in a village in Bihar, northern India, in January 2025. It measured 40.6 mm from snout to tail base, had no body pigment at all, and had eyes reduced to skin-covered spots.

The animal now has a formal name, Gangaichthys indonepalicus , and its describers place it in a new species and a new genus. Their paper appeared on 11 August in the journal ZooKeys , and the route by which they found it began on a phone.

The tip-off came from a phone

In the Introduction to their paper, Akshay Khandekar and his co-authors state plainly where the project started. “We came across a video posted on the social media platform TikTok in 2024 from the India-Nepal border area,” they write, “that showed a tiny, apparently stygobitic fish, with little melanin and reduced eyes, that had emerged from a borewell.”

A borewell, as the paper glosses it for readers who have never used one, is a machine-drilled shaft that reaches groundwater in an underground aquifer. Someone had pumped one, a strange pale fish had come out with the water, and the clip had gone up online.

The paper does not name the uploader. What the video did was point at a place.

A week of hand-pumping

Khandekar and his colleagues went to the Indo-Gangetic Plain in Bihar across 2024 and 2025 to try to find the animal. “We sampled more than 15 borewells by hand-pumping for approximately one week,” they write, “and were able to collect three specimens of the new species from two borewells.”

Two of those three arrived damaged. The holotype and one paratype came up the same well after roughly 2,000 to 2,500 litres had been pumped out of it; the holotype emerged intact, and the other fish sustained damage during pumping and died immediately. A third, fragmentary, came from another hand pump about 900 metres north two days later.

That one undamaged animal is why the osteology exists.

It was photographed alive, then euthanised, fixed, and taken to the National Centre for Biological Sciences in Bengaluru, where Sunil Prabhakar ran it through a micro-CT scanner in February 2025 without contrast agents.

A diagnosis built from one animal

The scan is where most of the counts come from. The fish has 64 vertebrae in total, 28 abdominal and 36 caudal, along with 37 dorsal fin-rays, 35 anal fin-rays, six caudal fin-rays, and a single pectoral fin-ray that the scan itself did not resolve: the osteology records no ossified pectoral ray at all.

It is the combination that the paper calls unique, not the individual figures. Several of these counts overlap with other members of the family Chaudhuriidae, the earthworm eels: the paper describes the new fish as similar to Pillaia in total, abdominal and caudal vertebrae and in dorsal and anal fin-rays, and similar to Chendol in dorsal and caudal fin-rays. The pectoral and caudal ray counts are the ones it calls non-overlapping against its nearest neighbour. No other chaudhuriid has all of these characters together, and the family’s members are all diminutive, none exceeding about 90 mm in total length.

The fish also appears to have no ribs, and here the paper explains a hedge its abstract already carries. The Discussion says that “though no ossified ribs were observed, the lack of contrast agents precludes the detection of weakly ossified or chondrified structures typical of miniaturized subterranean fishes.” With one intact specimen, the team could not scan again. The abstract and the diagnosis both call the absence of ribs apparent, and that qualifier is the authors’ own.

The other reductive traits are less ambiguous. Complete loss of body pigment and reduced eyes are what the paper calls classic reductive traits associated with hypogean environments, and it notes that such traits are often the result of convergent evolution driven by relaxed selection in dark, resource-poor habitats. They are evidence about environment; they say nothing about descent.

Sequencing has not caught up with the morphology

Only two species in the entire family have comparative mitochondrial CO1 sequence data available, one from each of two genera. Against those, the new fish’s CO1 sequence, deposited in GenBank as PZ760211, differs from Chaudhuria caudata by an average of 20.7 percent and from Pillaia indica by 22.2 percent, calculated as uncorrected p-distance. That is the basis for the abstract’s claim of more than 20 percent divergence. There is no comparative nuclear sequence data for the family at all.

The authors are explicit about what this does and does not settle. “The combination of unique morphological characters clearly distinguishes the new genus and species from other members of the Chaudhuriidae,” they write, “but a lack of comparative sequence data for the family prevents elucidation of generic inter-relationships and the position of the new genus within the family. This should be a priority for future work on the family and to confirm our recognition of Gangaichthys indonepalicus gen. et sp. nov. as a new genus.”

So the morphology, on their argument, carries both ranks. What is unresolved is where the new genus sits inside its family. They name the alternative reading themselves: the fish could be construed as a member of an expanded Chaudhuria , which they consider unlikely given the long branch length and the number of distinct morphological characters that separate it. That is a defended position, not a settled one, and it stays that way until more of the family has been sequenced.

An earlier blind eel that never counted

In 2008 Shrestha provisionally named a small blind eel-like fish, 33 mm long, from an unspecified locality in Narayani, southern Nepal, without designating a type specimen or pointing to any museum material.

Under the naming rules that makes “Neoanguilla nepalensis” a nomen nudum, a name with no standing. What that animal actually was remains unclear, and the new paper says so. It does rule out the simplest possibility: on Shrestha’s account that fish had 26 to 28 dorsal fin-rays against the Bihar fish’s 37, and had melanophores and a lateral line, both of which the new species lacks.

Gangaichthys indonepalicus is known from two closely spaced localities in Balgangwa village, Pashchim Champaran District, plus photographic records from Triveni in Nawalparasi District, Lumbini Province, Nepal. All of it sits inside 11 km in a straight line. The Nepali end of that range rests on photographs; no specimen has been collected there.

Pressure on the water below

The describers withheld the GPS coordinates, releasing them on request, to protect against illegal collection. They also name a second pressure, and it is upstream of anyone collecting.

India’s known hotspot for subterranean fish is the lateritic aquifer system of Kerala, in the south, with 11 species. This is the first subterranean fish from the alluvial aquifers of the Gangetic Basin, on the authors’ account, and it extends the known range of the earthworm eels roughly 500 km westward. Their recommendation is for targeted sampling of these fish across India, because what they call “dangerously high levels” of groundwater extraction and contamination are, on their account, “likely affecting” the subterranean fauna.

Nothing in this paper measures a decline, and it does not claim to. It establishes that something lives down there at all, in an aquifer under a heavily farmed plain, and that it reached science through a hand pump in a village and a phone.

title: Nepal, US plan high-level visits and other engagements next year - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepal, US plan high-level visits and other engagements next year  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Nepal and the United States are planning high-level visits and a series of other engagements next year as the two countries mark the 80th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations.

Nepal and the US established diplomatic ties in 1947. Officials at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said both sides are preparing a series of events, including high-level visits, trade and investment promotion, and cooperation in information technology and artificial intelligence, in Kathmandu and Washington to commemorate the anniversary.

Since there has been no high-level visit from the United States since 2002, Nepal is proposing a visit by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, among others, the officials said. Then-US Secretary of State Colin Powell paid an official visit to Nepal in January 2002. Since then, there have been several high-level visits from the Nepali side at the highest political level, but Washington’s visits are only represented by the undersecretary of state, parliamentarians and other officials.

Although details of the programmes and events are still under discussion, foreign ministry officials said Nepal wants to focus on exchanges between the business communities of the two countries, attracting US investment in diverse sectors, seeking a major infrastructure project and mobilising the Nepali diaspora in the United States.

Speaking at an event organised by the Centre for Social Innovation and Foreign Policy (CESIF) on Tuesday, Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said Nepal-US bilateral relations represent one of Nepal’s earliest and most enduring partnerships with the Western world.

“Our engagement has never been transactional; it is anchored in shared democratic values, mutual respect, and rich people-to-people connections,” Khanal said.

Highlighting US assistance to Nepal’s socioeconomic development, Khanal referred to American support for public health, including the landmark 1954 malaria control initiative and the 1958 National Malaria Eradication Programme, which helped open the fertile Tarai plains for settlement and agriculture. He also cited the contributions of Peace Corps volunteers, the Fulbright programme and academic exchanges.

“Today, this cooperation advances into high-impact infrastructure, as investments in clean energy transmission corridors and road connectivity. As Nepal prepares for its graduation from the Least Developed Country status, our bilateral relationship must evolve decisively beyond traditional development assistance,” he said.

Khanal said Nepal envisages a forward-looking partnership with the United States focused on three strategic pillars.

“First, we are advancing digital transformation by connecting Nepal’s talented youth and IT workforce with American innovation ecosystems and capital. Second, we are driving clean energy and climate resilience by developing sustainable hydropower, cross-border transmission grids, and protective measures for our fragile Himalayan ecosystem. Third, we are mobilising human capital and entrepreneurship by engaging the vibrant Nepali diaspora in the United States to foster technology transfer, trade links, and enterprise development,” he said.

At the same event, Scott Urbom, Chargé d’Affaires a.i. at the US Embassy in Kathmandu, highlighted the importance of shared democratic principles and continued economic collaboration in the technology and creative sectors.

He said investment in young Nepali talent and the US-Nepal relationship would contribute to long-term shared prosperity. Beyond technology, he said, US commitments remain anchored in vital physical and health infrastructure, including the more than $500 million Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC) compact to build high-voltage cross-border electricity transmission lines and upgrade strategic road corridors.

Urbom described Nepal’s recent elections as a remarkable generational shift and said the US Embassy in Kathmandu had engaged with more than 10,000 Nepali youths through different initiatives this year alone.

“In the last 79 years, we worked for shared prosperity and will work for trade, investment, technology, energy and other areas that will enable Nepal as a strong and prosperous nation,” Urbom said.

Former UN Ambassador Prof Dr Jayaraj Acharya highlighted how US-backed malaria eradication efforts reshaped the Terai’s economy, how bipartisan Congressional diplomacy supported Nepal’s democratic restoration in 1990, and why constitutional checks and balances and educational exchanges remain important anchors of democratic governance.

Reshu Aryal, a member of the National Planning Commission, reflected on the shared democratic values and people-to-people ties between Nepal and the United States, emphasising the role of younger generations in strengthening democratic institutions.

She highlighted the need to understand emerging Gen Z political realities, strengthen civic maturity and accountability, and move away from feudal modes of political thinking towards an empowered citizenry.

title: Dhurmus-Suntali Launch New U.S.-Based Comedy Series Focused on Nepali Diaspora Life - nepyork
description: Dhurmus-Suntali Launch New U.S.-Based Comedy Series Focused on Nepali Diaspora Life  nepyork
publisher.title: nepyork
full_article:
Popular Nepali comedy duo Sitaram Kattel, known as Dhurmus, and Kunjana Ghimire, known as Suntali, have produced a new comedy series in the United States.

The series, produced around Raleigh, North Carolina, focuses on the lives, experiences and challenges of Nepalis living in the United States. It is produced under Dhurmus-Suntali Media and will stream every Friday on the Dhurmus Suntali YouTube channel.

The program is scheduled to air at 8:15 p.m. Nepal time every Friday, while viewers in the United States can watch it at 10:30 a.m. Friday.

Filmed Across North Carolina

Kattel, who directed the series, said filming took place in Raleigh, Cary, Holly Springs, High Point and Greensboro, North Carolina.

The title comes from one of Dhurmus’ popular catchphrases from his earlier comedy work. Kattel and Ghimire will reprise their signature characters, Dhurmus and Suntali.

Senior comedian Mohan Mishra also appears in a leading role. Mishra, known as an actor and director for popular comedy programs including Hosh Prasad and Mr. Funtus , is returning to acting after a long break.

Cast and Crew

The cast includes Dinesh Karki, Shankar Raj Wagle, Sanyam Lamichhane, Monika Chaulagai, Chuda Dhimal, Dharma Bharati and Subhadra Acharya.

The series also marks the acting debut of Kattel and Ghimire’s daughter, Subihani Kattel, as a child performer. Veteran Nepali film actor Jeevan Luitel, who lives in the United States, will make a guest appearance after a lengthy break from the screen.

Raju KC handled cinematography. Ashish Aviral provided vocals, Prakash Punj wrote the lyrics, Rajendra Bajgai composed the music and Rajendra Manandhar edited the series.

Filming of the new Dhurmus-Suntali comedy series takes place in the Raleigh area of North Carolina.

Focus on Nepali Diaspora Life

The production team said the series will go beyond entertainment, using comedy and satire to portray the realities of Nepali immigrant life in the United States.

The story explores Nepalis’ struggles, opportunities, achievements and daily experiences abroad, as well as the Nepali community’s social and cultural environment. It addresses language barriers, cultural adjustment, work and business experiences, family relationships, the views of younger generations and efforts to preserve Nepali identity.

Madhav Dhakal, a former Nepali film producer and businessman based in High Point, North Carolina, praised the pair for pursuing regular creative work while living abroad.

“Starting regular artistic work from abroad is itself commendable,” Dhakal said. “It is not an ordinary matter for Sitaram ji to continue in this field. We will all provide our support and cooperation.”

Since moving to the United States, Kattel and Ghimire have remained active in media production, producing advertisements for about a dozen Nepali businesses and organizations. Kattel said additional advertisements and music videos are currently being filmed and produced.

“Our viewers will now be able to watch our serial regularly,” Kattel said. “Wherever we live, we want to convey the message that we can continue our art and creative work.”

उत्तरी कैरोलिना भर में फिल्माया

नेपयॉर्क कें मुफ्त मे सब्सक्राइब करू आब, अहां यू.एस.वीजा, ग्रीन कार्ड, आ सब आप्रवासन समाचारक कें कोनों अपडेट कें संग-संग आवास, कर, स्वास्थ्य देखभाल, आ बहुत किछु पर आवश्यक जानकारी आ संसाधनक कें सेहो छूटि नहिं जायब. एकरा सब के सीधा अपन इनबॉक्स में पहुंचा दियौ। ईमेल पता एतय दर्ज करू... सब्सक्राइब करय लेल एतय क्लिक करू

ई शीर्षक धुर्मुस केरऽ एगो लोकप्रिय कैचफ्रेज स॑ मिललऽ छै जे हुनकऽ पहिने के हास्य कृति स॑ छै । कट्टल आ घिमिरे अपन सिग्नेचर किरदार धुर्मुस आ सुनतली कए दोबारा प्रस्तुत करताह ।

वरिष्ठ हास्य अभिनेता मोहन मिश्रा सेहो अग्रणी भूमिका मे अबैत छथि । होश प्रसाद आ मिस्टर फंटस सहित लोकप्रिय हास्य कार्यक्रम के अभिनेता आ निर्देशक के रूप में जानल जाय वाला मिश्रा बहुत दिन के ब्रेक के बाद अभिनय में वापसी क रहल छैथ।

कलाकार आ चालक दल

कलाकार मे दिनेश कार्की, शंकर राज वागले, संयाम लामिछाने, मोनिका चौलागाई, चूड़ा धीमाल, धर्म भारती आ सुभद्रा आचार्य शामिल छथि ।

ई धारावाहिक म॑ कटेल आरू घिमिरे केरऽ बेटी सुबिहानी कटेल केरऽ अभिनय केरऽ शुरुआत भी बाल कलाकार के रूप म॑ करलऽ गेलऽ छै । अमेरिका मे रहनिहार नेपाली फिल्मक दिग्गज अभिनेता जीवन लुइटेल पर्दा सँ लंबा समय धरि विरामक बाद अतिथिक रूप मे नजरि आओताह ।

राजू केसी छायांकन संभालने छलाह। आशीष अविराल स्वर प्रदान केलनि, प्रकाश पुंज गीत लिखलनि, राजेन्द्र बाजगाई संगीतक रचना केलनि आ राजेन्द्र मानन्धर एहि धारावाहिकक संपादन केलनि ।

धुर्मुस-सुंताली केरऽ नयका कॉमेडी सीरीज केरऽ फिल्मांकन नॉर्थ कैरोलिना केरऽ रेले इलाका म॑ होय रहलऽ छै ।

नेपाली प्रवासी जीवन पर ध्यान देब

निर्माण टीम के कहनाय छनि जे ई धारावाहिक मनोरंजन सं आगू बढ़ि क' अमेरिका मे नेपाली आप्रवासी जीवन के यथार्थ के चित्रण करय लेल हास्य आ व्यंग्य के प्रयोग करत.

कथा मे विदेश मे नेपाली लोकनिक संघर्ष, अवसर, उपलब्धि आ दैनिक अनुभवक संग-संग नेपाली समुदायक सामाजिक आ सांस्कृतिक परिवेशक खोज कयल गेल अछि । एहि मे भाषाक बाधा, सांस्कृतिक समायोजन, कार्य आ व्यवसायिक अनुभव, पारिवारिक संबंध, नव पीढ़ीक विचार आ नेपाली पहिचानक संरक्षणक प्रयास केँ संबोधित कयल गेल अछि ।

नॉर्थ कैरोलिना के हाई प्वाइंट में रहय वाला पूर्व नेपाली फिल्म निर्माता आ व्यवसायी माधव ढकाल विदेश में रहैत नियमित रूप स रचनात्मक काज करय लेल एहि जोड़ी के प्रशंसा केलनि।

धकाल कहलनि जे, विदेश स नियमित कलात्मक काज शुरू करब अपने आप मे सराहनीय अछि। ओ कहलनि जे, सीताराम जी के लेल एहि क्षेत्र मे आगू बढ़ब कोनो साधारण बात नहि अछि, हम सब अपन सहयोग आ सहयोग देब।”

अमेरिका आबि गेलाक बाद सं कट्टल आ घिमिरे मीडिया निर्माण मे सक्रिय रहलाह, लगभग एक दर्जन नेपाली व्यवसाय आ संस्थाक विज्ञापनक निर्माण करैत छथि । कटेल कहलनि जे, एखन अतिरिक्त विज्ञापन आ म्यूजिक वीडियो के फिल्मांकन आ निर्माण भ रहल अछि।

कटेल कहला जे आब हमर दर्शक हमर धारावाहिक नियमित रूप स देख सकैत छथि। “हम सब जतय रहैत छी, ई संदेश देबय चाहैत छी जे हम सब अपन कला आ रचनात्मक काज के आगू बढ़ा सकैत छी।”

title: ‘His feet are his pillars’: Nepal para swimmer gives all for Asian glory - Kuwait Times
description: ‘His feet are his pillars’: Nepal para swimmer gives all for Asian glory  Kuwait Times
publisher.title: Kuwait Times
full_article:
Every morning Harka Man Gharti slices into the blue water of a swimming pool in Nepal’s capital Kathmandu, chasing a dream that stretches far beyond its 25 metres. Unlike the swimmers around him who rely on long strokes of their arms, Gharti powers through his legs and torso because he does not have arms.

The 21-year-old is training with three other disabled swimmers who will represent Nepal in the Asian Para Games in Japan in October, chasing medals despite limited resources in the Himalayan country. “It is not my hope, it is my target,” Gharti told AFP after finishing a gruelling session. “Just for a medal, I am giving everything... every possible thing.”

A decade ago an electrocution accident near a hydroelectric project in his native Baglung district in western Nepal changed his life forever, costing him both arms. The tragedy that could have ended his ambitions instead helped forge his extraordinary determination. What began as an experiment with competitive swimming in 2020 soon became a passion and a career pathway.

“I love everything about swimming, whether competitive or just for enjoying,” he said. At the hostel where he lives in Kathmandu a row of medals hangs above his bed, proof of a remarkable journey. During training he concentrates on his technique and body position in the water. On race days a different instinct takes over. “I don’t really think about the techniques or my body alignment,” he said. “I just go hard. I just push fast and I just want to push power. That’s it. I just think about speed and for speed I just kick harder and harder.”

Nepalese para-swimmer Harka Man Gharti (left) using his toes to eat a meal at his residence in Kathmandu. Nepalese para-swimmer Harka Man Gharti using his mouth to write at his residence in Kathmandu. Nepalese para-swimmer Harka Man Gharti using his toes to draw at his residence in Kathmandu. Nepalese para-swimmers Harka Man Gharti (right) and Member Singi Syangba taking a break during a training session in Kathmandu. Nepalese para-swimmers Harka Man Gharti (left), Jenisha Kadayat (second left), Sirjana Sarki (second right) and Member Singi Syangba posing for a photograph during a training session in Kathmandu. --AFP photos Nepalese para-swimmer Harka Man Gharti taking part in a training session in Kathmandu.

Leg power

At last year’s Para Swimming World Series in Japan, Gharti’s times met the minimum qualifying standards for the Asian Para Games, earning him a chance to compete on one of the biggest sporting stages. He will participate in the S5 classification, including the 50-metre freestyle. China’s Guo Jincheng holds the men’s 50m freestyle record at 29.33 seconds in the category. Sports facilities in Nepal are modest by international standards.

Para athletes in the country often face limited funding, scarce specialized infrastructure and a lack of competitive opportunities. His coach, Subha Shrestha, believes Gharti’s greatest strength lies not in what he has lost, but in what he has built. “When we don’t have even a single finger we feel the impact,” Shrestha said. “But he is working so hard with no hands.

Nepalese para-swimmer Harka Man Gharti being assisted by his coach Subah Shrestha during a training session in Kathmandu. Nepalese para-swimmer Harka Man Gharti resting at his residence in Kathmandu. Nepalese para-swimmer Harka Man Gharti using his toes to operate mobile phone at his residence in Kathmandu. Nepalese para-swimmers Harka Man Gharti (left) and Member Singi Syangba taking a break during a training session in Kathmandu. Nepalese para-swimmer Harka Man Gharti swimming during a training session in Kathmandu. Nepalese para-swimmer Harka Man Gharti using his toes to brush teeth at his residence in Kathmandu.

“His feet are his pillars, his legs are very powerful.” The wider significance of Gharti’s quest is not lost on Nepal’s para swimming community. The nation has had only one Asian Para Games medallist, taekwondo athlete Palesha Goverdhan, who won bronze last time out before also claiming a medal in Paralympics. For many years Nepali athletes have arrived at major competitions with modest expectations.

“In Nepal they often say that we go only for the sake of participation,” said Saroj Shrestha, president of the National Para Swimming Association of Nepal. “But Harka and we both dream to do something in swimming that even able-bodied athletes have not been able to achieve.”

Inspiring others

Back on the pool deck, Gharti’s ambitions extend beyond sport. Having recently completed high school, he plans to study computer science. He navigates a computer with his toes, displaying the same determination that has become central to his swimming. “Swimming is a platform for me where it is on me whether I can make my life better or not. “Because if I hit a world record then of course my life will be better,” he said. “Only then can I speak of inspiring anyone else.” — AFP

title: NTB brings 35 travel creators together to reshape Nepal’s tourism story - The Tourism Times
description: NTB brings 35 travel creators together to reshape Nepal’s tourism story  The Tourism Times
publisher.title: The Tourism Times
full_article:
KATHMANDU: The Nepal Tourism Board has brought together 35 travel video makers, vloggers and social media influencers to discuss how Nepal can promote its tourism more effectively and authentically in the digital age.

The interaction, organised by the NTB at the Ministry of Culture, Tourism and Civil Aviation, focused on ways to present Nepal's destinations and experiences to wider international audiences through digital storytelling.

Minister for Culture, Tourism and Civil Aviation Khadak Raj Paudel, Nepal Tourism Board Chairman and Tourism Ministry Secretary Mukund Prasad Niraula, and NTB Officiating Chief Executive Officer Hikmat Singh Ayer attended the interaction.

Minister Paudel stressed the need to showcase the “real Nepal”, saying the country's tourism story should go beyond its mountains, landscapes and heritage to highlight its people, hospitality, culture, stories and everyday interactions that make visitors' experiences memorable.

NTB Officiating CEO Ayer welcomed the content creators and called for their continued support in promoting Nepal's destinations and tourism experiences to audiences around the world.

The creators shared their experiences and discussed challenges in promoting Nepal, including the need for stronger coordination among government agencies and stakeholders, better synchronisation of promotional efforts and more effective use of the tourism-related content already being produced.

The discussion also highlighted the changing nature of destination marketing, with participants stressing that tourism promotion increasingly depends on compelling and credible stories rather than conventional advertising alone.

The NTB said the interaction was aimed at strengthening collaboration with creators who are already travelling across Nepal, producing visual content and sharing their experiences with audiences at home and abroad.

full_article:
The rape and murder of a three-year-old girl in Nepal sparked parliamentary demands for the death penalty



Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.



NEW DELHI: The rape and murder of a three-year-old girl in Nepal’s Bara district, around 25km from Raxaul in Bihar, triggered demands for the death penalty in parliament after days of protests, even as the principal suspect is a 16-year-old boy who, if convicted, would be sentenced under Nepal’s juvenile justice law. Lawmakers sought constitutional changes to allow capital punishment for heinous crimes, while RSP law minister Sobita Gautam and home minister Sudan Gurung told parliament that the govt could not introduce it without first amending the Constitution.The girl disappeared from Jeetpur-Simara on Aug 16 and her body was recovered two days later from an abandoned house near her home, leading to demonstrations in Simara, Kathmandu and other parts of Nepal. Police identified her teen neighbour as the principal suspect and widened the investigation, taking nine people into custody amid questions over whether officers had responded quickly enough after the family reported her missing.The killing dominated parliament proceedings, with ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) lawmaker Afsana Banu demanding an amendment to Article 16(2), which prohibits capital punishment, and calling for Nepal to reconsider its international commitments against the death penalty.“No international treaty or law can stand above citizens’ safety. Concern for the human rights of criminals cannot come at the cost of victims’ rights and justice,” she said, urging her govt to amend the Constitution to allow death penalty for heinous crimes.Other RSP lawmakers questioned whether the existing legal framework provided adequate punishment in such cases. Anushka Shrestha said, “A person should not escape severe punishment for a heinous crime merely because the perpetrator is a minor,” while arguing that punishment for rape needed review. Shraddha Kunwar raised a separate constitutional argument, asking whether parliament should focus only on the prohibition on death penalty or also ensure women’s constitutional right to live with dignity.Gautam, however, told parliament that Article 16(2) explicitly barred Nepal from making any law providing for capital punishment and pointed to the country's international human rights commitments. “No matter how intense public anger becomes, our govt cannot legislate beyond the Constitution,” she said. Nepal constitutionally abolished capital punishment in 1990 and retained the prohibition in its 2015 Constitution.The suspect’s age presents a separate legal issue even as lawmakers debate capital punishment. Under Nepal’s Children Act, 2018, anyone below 18 is dealt with under juvenile law, and an offender aged 16 to below 18 can receive two-thirds of the punishment prescribed for an adult. For adults, Nepal’s criminal law provides for imprisonment for the remainder of natural life for murder committed after rape, the maximum punishment available under the existing constitutional framework.Following days of protests, govt reached a three-point agreement with the victim’s family and formed a seven-member Garima Nyaya Sankalpa Samiti under law ministry, giving it seven days to recommend changes concerning sexual violence and offences against women and children.
